paragraphs.heading: What counts as a fish
paragraphs.text: A fish is a vertebrate that lives in water, breathes with gills and has a tough skull, the cranium, guarding its brain. Many fish have fins that keep them on course and push them along. Most are cold-blooded, so their body temperature rises and falls with the water around them. A few large, fast swimmers such as the white shark and tuna can keep their core warmer. The science of fish is called ichthyology.

paragraphs.heading: A huge and varied group
paragraphs.text: More than 33,000 living species of fish are known, more than amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals put together. Most of them are ray-finned fishes, a class that alone makes up about half of all living vertebrates. Within it, the teleosts, fish that can push their jaws forward, account for about 96% of living fish species. Sizes run from the whale shark at 16 metres down to tiny teleosts only 8 millimetres long, such as Paedocypris progenetica.

paragraphs.heading: The first fish
paragraphs.text: Fishlike animals such as Haikouichthys enter the fossil record in the Cambrian explosion, some 530 million years ago. The earliest fish were small filter feeders. Later came the ostracoderms, the earliest fish with gills dedicated to breathing and with paired fins, which wore heavy bony plates as armour against invertebrate predators. The first jawed fish, the placoderms, appeared in the Silurian and became much more varied in the Devonian, the period known as the Age of Fishes.

paragraphs.heading: Bony fish take over
paragraphs.text: Bony fish carry a swim bladder, and later ones also have skeletons made of bone. They became the leading group after an extinction at the end of the Devonian wiped out the placoderms, which had been the top predators. Bony fish split into two branches, the lobe-finned and the ray-finned fishes. During the Carboniferous, lobe-finned fish gave rise to the tetrapods, four-limbed vertebrates that mostly live on land, and their air-breathing lungs correspond to the swim bladder.

paragraphs.heading: Why fish is not one class
paragraphs.text: Older books put every fish into a single class called Pisces, but that class is no longer used in formal classification. The reason is that tetrapods descend from fish. Any group that includes all bony fish therefore also includes the tetrapods, so fish without them is what biologists call a paraphyletic group. To make fish one complete branch, tetrapods would have to count as specialised fish, and fish would simply mean vertebrate. The reference book Fishes of the World accepts this, calling tetrapods, humans included, modified bony fishes.

paragraphs.heading: Fish, fishes and people
paragraphs.text: In biology, fish and fishes mean different things: fish names one or more individual animals, while fishes names different species. People have relied on fish since prehistoric times, especially as food. Fish are caught in the wild or raised in ponds and ocean cages. They are also caught for sport, kept in aquariums and garden ponds, and have appeared as gods, religious symbols and subjects of art, books and films.
